A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PRIME. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL training results, seven-benchmark evaluations and ablations, including Tables 2–3 and Figures 3–13.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds original scaling, runtime, reward-model-size, loss-function and baseline-comparison results.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the default implicit-reward, advantage-estimation and policy-update procedures remain unchanged. Appendix C.2 introduces and tests an alternative DPO loss for updating the PRM, while retaining CE as the default.

E1.justification: v2 adds AIME 2025 evaluation in Table 5. Additional comparisons use MATH training data and the DeepScaleR training setting in Appendices B.6–B.7. The original seven benchmarks and documented SFT/RL data collections remain, with coverage still centered on mathematical and coding reasoning.

E2.justification: v2 adds a reproduced VinePPO comparison and comparisons with DeepScaleR checkpoints in Tables 6–7, substantially extending the evaluated alternatives beyond the existing RL algorithms. VinePPO was only cited in v1. DeepScaleR comparisons use reported results and an estimated training curve; the original comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 800 rollout steps, 16 responses per prompt instead of four, and 3B/7B/14B reward models with a fixed 7B policy. Additional protocols include matched 96-step RhoMath-1.1B training, 330-step training with an 8k response limit under the DeepScaleR setting, and avg@16 evaluation at temperature 0.3. The original main-experiment settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial tests of whether gains persist with more training and rollouts, whether reward-model capacity matters, and whether CE versus DPO PRM training changes performance. Runtime profiling also examines computational overhead. Earlier filtering, initialization, reference-model, single/double-forward and Zero analyses are retained, including relocated appendix material.

E5.justification: Table 12 newly reports avg@16 evaluation, adding explicit averaging over 16 sampled responses for AIME 2024 and AMC. This does not establish repeated independent RL training runs. The disclosed SFT seed remains 42, and no new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: The original main and RL-algorithm tables retain their scores, but v2 adds substantial scaling, timing, model-size, loss-choice and avg@16 results. For example, Table 6 reports 18.8% versus 18.4% validation accuracy and 1.22 versus 13.94 hours for PRIME versus VinePPO at 96 steps. These are newly reported experiments, not improvements to the unchanged original scores.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds a soft-Q expression, mathematical reasoning about cancellation of prompt-dependent reward offsets, and a potential-based reward-shaping argument at gamma=1. These extend the justification of the existing formulation; the original advantage equations remain, and no substantial new theorem-and-proof development is supplied.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: online implicit PRMs trained from outcome labels, elimination of dedicated PRM pretraining, compatibility with multiple RL algorithms, and improved efficiency and reasoning performance. The headline performance and data-efficiency claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of the method through Appendix C's discussion of reward parameterization, loss normalization and reward shaping. It adds interpretations concerning limited benefits from larger PRMs and reduced relative overhead for long responses. Appendix A newly states the 32B experimental boundary and shorter ablation budgets; the earlier Zero-training saturation discussion is retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds hardware specifications, component-level timing, CPU-offloading information and resource budgets for new comparisons. Existing training hyperparameters and preprocessing instructions remain. v1's public project/model/data link is removed, while v2 instead states that code is provided in supplementary material.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to DeepScaleR, Rho-1, potential-based reward shaping and maximum-entropy RL, and removes the Meta 2024 reference. Appendix C clarifies relationships to DPO and entropy-regularized RL. The main positioning around scalable online dense rewards remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The document is extensively reorganized: imitation warmup moves into Appendix D; reference-model, single/double-forward and Zero studies move into Appendix B; detailed alternative advantage formulas also move out of the main text. v2 adds limitations, ethics, reproducibility and theoretical-discussion sections, alongside prose compression and author-list changes.

P2.justification: Numerous displays are relocated and resized, including v1 Figure 1 becoming appendix Figure 12 and v1 Table 3 becoming appendix Table 4. v2 adds scaling plots, runtime and comparison tables, and loss-ablation displays. Figure 17 presents the existing dense-versus-sparse comparison against wall time; retained plots also receive caption and legend revisions.

improvement.justification: v2 materially strengthens the central efficiency argument, which in v1 relied mainly on training-step counts, through runtime profiling and a matched VinePPO comparison. Longer-training, larger-rollout and PRM-size/loss studies also address important robustness gaps. These gains outweigh limited shortcomings: DeepScaleR comparisons use estimated curves and different hardware/budgets, Table 2 implies approximately 28% overhead rather than the stated 24%, and direct public resource access information is reduced.
